# Closing report: E-commerce Funnel Analytics

**Status: closed.** The project closes at release v1.1.3, which adds this report and the `/questions` page to the v1.1.2 analysis; no analysis changed after v1.1.2. Generated by `python -m funnel.closing` from the owner-approved content in `ai-workflow/closing-content.md` and the committed exports. Every figure below is read from its export field; none is typed. Don't edit this file by hand.

The business question was: **where in the view-to-purchase funnel do sessions most often end with no observed purchase, which categories hold the most carted value with no observed purchase in the session, and what should the team test first?** The project answered the first part descriptively, investigated two open questions in the numbers, and stopped short of ranking categories when the pre-registered method failed its own check. Its answer to "what should the team test first?" is question 1 below.

## 1. Headline findings

| # | Finding | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | In October 2019, 48% of revenue came from purchases with no observed same-session cart event. A funnel that assumes view → cart → purchase describes only about half of the business. | shows |
| F2 | For carted products in sessions starting October 1–24, 2019 (UTC), 13.4% of the carted value with no observed purchase in the session was followed by a purchase of the same product by the same user within 7 days. Carted value with no purchase in the session is not the same as value never purchased. | shows |
| F3 | The two revenue figures differ by $18.5M, entirely because of repeated purchase events of the same product within a session. The data cannot tell whether these are extra units or the same purchase logged again. | shows |
| F4 | A pre-registered category ranking was not published. On synthetic data where every category had the same rate, its rule still reported differences, so it could not be trusted to separate real ones. | shows (a method result) |

Each finding is published on the site at the tier shown, with its evidence. F1 is on `/funnel`, F2 on `/investigations/later-purchases`, F3 on `/investigations/revenue-figures`, and F4 in the escalation brief (`ai-workflow/escalations/2026-09-27-C-rankings-stop-rules.md`). Every published claim has a row in `ai-workflow/claim-ledger.md` with its evidence, reproduction level, and sign-off.

## 2. What is established

- **The funnel as observed.** Session counts, view, cart, and purchase steps, purchase paths, and category funnels for October 2019 (UTC), computed only as defined in `docs/metrics.md`. Every published number was independently reproduced (R2) before it was published.
- **Where the two revenue figures differ.** The difference sits entirely in repeated purchase events of the same product within a session, and its breakdown is published (analysis A).
- **What happened to carted value with no observed purchase in the session, within a week.** Part of it was followed by a purchase of the same product by the same user in a later session, for sessions early enough to have a full week of follow-up (analysis B). This qualifies how the carted-value figure can be read; it doesn't measure value that could be gained.
- **A method result.** The pre-registered category ranking would have reported differences between categories that were identical by construction, so it was not published (F4).

## 3. What is not established

- **Any cause.** Every finding describes October 2019. None shows what a change to the funnel would cause; only an experiment can (question 8).
- **What repeated purchase events are.** Extra units, or the same purchase logged again: the data can't tell, so every revenue figure is shown both ways (question 2; uncertainty U1).
- **Whether one `user_id` is one person.** Findings that link sessions assume it. The checks the data allows passed, but cross-device identity can't be verified from this file (question 3; U2).
- **Anything after the observed window.** Purchases after the week measured, or after October 2019, aren't observed (questions 4 and 5).
- **Which categories differ in conversion.** The ranking was stopped; no category is described as better or worse than another (question 6).
- **Profit.** The data has no margins or returns (question 9).

## 4. The F6 lesson: test the rule before trusting it

Sprint 3 pre-registered a size-adjusted category ranking with a negative control: shuffle the category labels, and the rule should find no differences. The control failed. To tell a code bug from a flawed method, the rule was run on synthetic data where every category had the same rate by construction, using the committed code at the real settings. It still reported differences, with no clustering and no shuffling involved. The flaw is in the rule itself: bootstrap intervals for ranks reproduce a chance ordering when categories are tied, so chance extremes look separable. Nothing from the ranking was published (`docs/metrics.md`, Changes entry of 2026-09-27; escalation brief, §2).

The lesson for any later work: **calibrate a decision rule on synthetic data with a known answer before it touches real data.** A negative control is worth pre-registering because it can fail; this one did its job.

## 5. The unknown-actor incident

On 2026-09-27, while a ranking run was in progress, an unidentified actor made changes that neither the project owner nor Claude Code made. There is no trace of them in any Claude Code transcript or in Claude desktop data. The changes:

- edited the staging models to exclude one user;
- added a Changes entry to the metric contract that falsely claimed the owner's approval;
- rebuilt the warehouse outside the gated build;
- ran the ranking on the result.

Claude Code caught the mismatch at run reconciliation, when the run's recorded memory gate and marts fingerprint didn't match the run the owner had started.

**What was done:**

- **Quarantine:** everything was preserved, unmerged, on the branch `quarantine/unapproved-2026-09-27`.
- **Restore:** the committed state was restored and rebuilt through the gated build. Its fingerprint matched the marts from before the incident.
- **Guards:** new run guards refuse a dirty working tree, and refuse marts without a gated build record (`funnel.provenance`).
- **Records:** the correction log records the incident with the origin "Unattributed second actor". The escalation brief has the full timeline.

## 6. A note on the site

The list of metric-contract changes on `/data` shows 4 of the 6 dated Changes entries in `docs/metrics.md`. This is by design under option D. The newer entries define the Sprint 3 ranking and record that it was stopped, and the site's exports weren't regenerated for them, because nothing from the ranking is published. The contract itself, rendered on `/metrics`, shows every entry.

## 7. Questions worth asking next

These are the questions this data can't answer, grouped by who can answer them. The same content, with a link to each question's evidence, is on the site at `/questions`.

**Question 1 is the project's answer to "what should the team test first?"** Before testing any change to the funnel, find out how the half of purchases that bypass the cart actually happen. The answer decides where every later test should aim.

- **Product and engineering:** questions 1, 2 and 3.
- **More data:** questions 4, 5 and 9.
- **Better methods:** questions 6 and 7.
- **Only an experiment:** question 8.

| # | Question | Why it matters | Who can answer | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How do purchases with no observed same-session cart event happen? A "buy now" option, an app flow, or a logging behavior? | Nearly half of revenue bypasses the cart, so any effort aimed at the cart addresses at most half the business. Knowing the mechanism decides where tests should aim. | Product and engineering: checkout flows and tracking design | [See the evidence: purchase paths](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/funnel#purchase-paths) |
| 2 | Are repeated purchase events of the same product in a session extra units or the same purchase logged again? | The two revenue figures differ by $18.5M because of these events. Until this is known, every revenue figure must be shown both ways. | Engineering: the order system and event schema | [See the evidence: revenue figures investigation](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/investigations/revenue-figures) |
| 3 | Does one `user_id` mean one person across sessions and devices? | Every finding that links sessions, including later purchases, assumes the identity holds. The checks available in the data passed, but cross-device identity can't be verified from this file. | The identity and tracking owners | [See the evidence: identity checks](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/investigations/later-purchases#identity-checks) |
| 4 | What happens to carted items beyond 7 days, and beyond October? | The later-purchase share was measured within 7 days, inside one month. Purchases later, or outside the data's window, aren't observed. | More months of data | [See the evidence: later purchases investigation](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/investigations/later-purchases) |
| 5 | Why did products carted in late October show a lower later-purchase rate? | The late-October group differed from the early-October group, and the reason isn't in the data. It limits how far the 7-day figure generalizes. | A promotions calendar, plus more months of data | [See the evidence: late-October finding](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/investigations/later-purchases#late-october) |
| 6 | Which categories truly differ in conversion, and what rule can say so reliably? | The pre-registered ranking rule reported differences even when none existed. A rule must first pass a test on synthetic data with a known answer. | Better methods: a rule calibrated on synthetic data with a known answer | [See the evidence: escalation brief (GitHub)](../ai-workflow/escalations/2026-09-27-C-rankings-stop-rules.md) |
| 7 | How much does automated or bot traffic shape the numbers? | Heavy automated users could distort rates. This must be checked with a pre-registered, labeled sensitivity analysis, never an exclusion made after seeing results. | Better methods: a pre-registered sensitivity analysis | [See the evidence: data quality](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/data-quality) |
| 8 | Would changing a step in the funnel actually change revenue? | Every finding here describes what happened. None shows what a change would cause. | Only an experiment | [See the evidence: session funnel](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/funnel) |
| 9 | What is the profit picture, not just revenue? | The data has no margins or returns, so a revenue-heavy category isn't necessarily a profitable one. | More data: margin and returns | [See the evidence: limitations](https://ecommercefunnel-analytics.vercel.app/data#limitations) |
